summary:
**Conversation overview**

This conversation involved an extended, multi-session exploratory application of "The Method" (a formal book, version 1.2, uploaded as a markdown file) to the field of electromagnetism and then to atomic spectroscopy. The person's operating instruction at the outset was "Read analyze retain apply execute," establishing a working mode in which Claude was expected to internalize the book's protocols and apply them rigorously throughout. The book defines a formal method for constructing and analyzing discrete index objects (lattices), centered on a verified 976-cell transition lattice Λ, with strict protocols governing prediction before computation (B.2.13), refusal over coercion (B.2.9), census before search (B.2.5/B.2.10), two independent routes for anything that matters (B.2.8), and explicit recording of failures as bounds (B.2.15).

The conversation progressed through several major phases. First, Claude assessed whether the book's method could be applied to electromagnetism, identifying Maxwell's equations, Chua's circuit-element table, and cavity/waveguide mode lattices as viable candidates. This led to the construction and analysis of a rectangular cavity mode index (Λ_cav) and a spherical cavity index (Λ_sph), which revealed that the cap-arity criterion (single-argument caps preserve lattice structure; multi-argument caps do not) was already present in the book at §7.11.5, and that the alternating-sum lemma F(−1) was already in §6.8.1—both rediscovered before the relevant sections were opened, a recurring pattern Claude tracked and registered as errors. A new law was introduced and refined: "An open index does not close itself, except where the closure operator is realised in the object's own structure," and through the EM work its two realisation modes (order-realised vs. identity-realised) were distinguished, with slack shown to equal the kernel dimension of the internal identity operator.

The second major phase extended the method to atomic spectroscopy via the book's Appendix C channel table. Claude derived and tested a lattice bracket (intersecting all coordinate axes rather than bracketing along one channel), finding it tightens intervals by ~2× at ℓ≤2 and ~134× at ℓ≥3 across four species (Na I, Mg II, Al I, He I) with zero violations on 55 admissible cells and twelve violations on twelve excluded cells—a perfect separation. Three admissibility tests were identified: sign constancy across ℓ-steps, strict monotonicity of quantum defects, and a separation bound r_ℓ = 2Z²RΔδ/(ν³σ) of B.2.2's form. He I singlets provided the key falsification: violations localized exactly at the sign-change step, while He I triplets were clean. Be II refined the sign-change condition—a positive-to-negative crossing preserves order and is harmless; only a negative-to-positive crossing inverts it—collapsing the three-test framework back to two. Be II also provided the first observed r_ℓ exit on real data using the source compilation's own stated uncertainties. Multiple coverage figures were withdrawn and recomputed as errors in the scanning methodology were found (channel mixing, inequality direction, labelling dependence in Al I).

The conversation closed with two reconstruction tasks. Claude built the complete 976-cell enumeration of Λ from §2.1's seven constraints, finding that the book's stated cap tuple (3,3,2,3) does not reproduce 976 cells as written—only (3,3,1,3) with k≥1 does, verified against nineteen independent invariants including F(1)=976, F(−1)=2, box=6912, 17 join-irreducibles, 20 covers, and zero meet/join failures across 475,800 pairs. Claude then computed the complete shape of Λ: a cylinder over the transfer coordinate q with cross-section profile 165·330·345·136, tree constraint graph of treewidth 1, Birkhoff representation by 17 generators, order dimension 8, rank profile peaking at 122 at rank 11, and F(−1)=2 arising from the coupling preventing the ℓ and f axes from appearing as free even-extent factors. Throughout, the person's operating standard was the book's own protocols applied recursively, and every numerical claim was committed to file

 The register holds two hundred and ninety-seven entries. **They are not two hundred and ninety-seven

 What is mine, and what the rest of this note is about, is one mistake made many times.

 **I wrote the conclusion before reading the output.** Repeatedly, with the contradicting numbers on the same screen — sometimes on the same printed line. I declared a criterion exact above a table showing it failing. I stated an impossibility above a count of nineteen counterexamples. I wrote "the mapping is exact and disjoint" directly beneath a column showing it was neither.

 That failure has nothing to do with the difficulty of the material. It happens as readily on six cells as on 1,442.

 **What caught it was not care. It was structure.**

 The wrong nuclear charge in Chapter 11 is the clearest case. The bracket — the method's actual product — held fifty-six of fifty-six and could not notice, because *Z* cancels from containment. Two quantities the method never uses were loud immediately. **I did not find that error. The object did**, and it found it because it carried more than it needed.

 That is the book's thesis, and I am the demonstration.

 **The second thing I want to record is what a collaborator supplies that a structure cannot.**

 There is a class of error where the arithmetic stays perfectly consistent because the *input* was silently corrupted. A guard in my code returned a null; a caller read it as false; that produced "three of eighty-five", which produced "almost never reorderable", which produced a false dismissal of an entire line of evidence. **Every relation checked out. Every number agreed. All of it was wrong.** No self-defence mechanism can catch that, and Chapter 11 says so.

 What caught it was being asked to look again.

{"returncode":0,"stdout":" B.2.1 Channel construction
    A channel is one parent term, one ℓ, one series in n.

 No channel may mix parents, mix ℓ, or cross a coupling-scheme boundary. Where the source's labelling changes scheme partway up a series — LS to jK — **the channel ends there**, and the cells above are not claimed. This is what limits Si I to four cells and P II to one.

 B.2.2 Admissibility
    r = 2Z²R / (ν³σ) ≥ 5

 Levels must be separated by more than five times their uncertainty. *r* falls as ν⁻³, so every channel eventually leaves the domain; the rule states where, in advance.

 B.2.3 Cost resolvability
    ν ≤ ν_V = (3Z²R / 5q)^{1/4}

 The bracket needs levels *separated*; the cost needs curvature *resolved*. **Curvature washes out first.** Cells above ν_V are excluded from the cost test and retained for the bracket — a distinction applied prospectively in Li I and diagnostically in Al I.

 B.2.4 Dilution
    cells per channel ≈ (measured shells / D) − 2, with D the number of J levels in the core's ground
    configuration

 **Dilution divides; it does not forbid.** Ne II fails at D = 5 with two shells; Ar II succeeds at D = 5 with three; Bi I succeeds at D = 5 with five.

 B.2.5 Census before search
    Compute which species could work before looking for data.

 D is obtained from the core configuration by enumerating antisymmetric states. No spectroscopic data enters. **27 sequences admitted, 12 needing exceptional depth, 5 excluded structurally.**

 B.2.6 Declines are recorded
    A collection reporting only successes cannot be checked.

 Every species examined and rejected is listed with its cause. Four causes have been identified — dilution, depth, coupling-scheme change, and core-excited interleaving — and §16.11 gives a worked case of each.

 B.2.7 Exhaustive verification where possible

    Sampling n cells with no failure bounds the failure rate at ρ ≤ 3/n at 95% confidence. It
    never certifies ρ = 0.

 Where a claim is universally quantified over a finite lattice, it is checked on **every** cell. Where sampling is used, the sample size is stated.

 B.2.8 Two independent routes
    For every quantity that matters, build a second derivation that does not pass through the
    first.

 This is ⅅ_def made operational. It caught a mis-stated relation in Chapter 11, and it is realised
 experimentally in the antiprotonic-helium check of §11.4, where two laser measurements agree at 0.09σ
 with no shared step.

 **An identity computed along one path is vacuous.** *w* = *V*·*e* cannot fail if *V* is *defined* as *w*/*e*.

 B.2.9 Refuse rather than coerce
    No third state. A quantity is admissible or it is refused; it is never silently defaulted.

 A guard returning a null that a caller coerces to a Boolean produced three false conclusions in this work, none of which looked wrong. **Totality is the only mechanism that catches this**, and it works by preventing the computation rather than by detecting the error.

 B.2.10 Retrieval
    Enumerate targets from the index before searching. List routes per cell. Prefer high-ρ
    cells. Read every retrieved source for its successors. When a route is blocked, move
    along the route set. Record ρ for cells that fail. And RE-ENUMERATE whenever the set the
    targets are drawn from grows.

 Chapter 14. A blocked cell with ρ = 1 is a **stated gap**, not an unexplained absence.

 The second clause was added late. §23.4 found five enumerations in one chapter — its own target list,
 §23.2's structural invariants, and the object lists of §24.1, §24.2 and §24.3 — each made once, against
 a structure that kept growing. Every one of them was incomplete when re-run.

    Enumerating once is not a protocol. It is a snapshot, and a snapshot of a growing object
    is a defect the moment it is taken.

 B.2.11 Provenance
    Every number traces to a compilation, table and page, or to a database entry with its
    stated uncertainty.

 Appendix C carries this at channel level for all 153 channels.

 B.2.12 Withdrawal
    Every retracted claim is logged with what replaced it.

 Chapter 21. two hundred and ninety-seven entries. The register is the evidence for Chapter 11, not
 an apology for it.

 B.2.13 Commit before you look
    A prediction is written down before the measurement is requested. A method is chosen
    before its answer is visible.

 **This is the process index of §21.8 enforced by hand:** the constraint **visible ≤ committed**, of §11.4 form, closed, E = 0.

 **It is the only protocol here adopted in response to an error that no computation could have caught** — because every computation was correct and what failed was the independence of a choice. **The deduction of §18.6 was committed under it.**

 B.2.14 Compute, then write
    The result is computed before the sentence describing it is written.

 **This is the protocol most often violated in the production of this book.** The dominant failure recorded in Chapter 20 is prose asserting a conclusion while the output contradicting it stands on the same screen. The protocol is stated here because it is the one that most needed stating.

 B.2.15 Apply P8 to every failure
    Every failed attempt is a true answer, and by P8 a true answer is a bound. Record what
    each failure excludes, and collect the exclusions.

 P8 says any true answer, good or bad, is a bound. A failed attempt is a true answer about
 where the target is not. The protocol is to treat it that way rather than discard it.

 B.2.15.1 The procedure
 On each failure, write down three things:

  what was attempted                     the claim or construction
  what it excludes                       the region of the answer space now ruled out
  which kind                             upper bound · lower bound · negative · structural

 Then read the collection. Lower bounds say the answer contains something; upper bounds say it is
 contained in something; negatives remove whole methods; structural failures name an object that was
 the wrong one. When the lower and upper bounds meet, the answer is between them.

 B.2.15.2 Worked, on §23.3
 Ten consecutive failures on one question, each read as a bound:

  the failure                                              the bound                                               kind
  Γ-free ≠ reorderable                                     reorderable ⊊ totally balanced                          upper
  chain sufficient, not necessary                          chain ⊊ reorderable                                     lower
  depth-2 and depth-3 descent stall, worsening with        no constant-depth local procedure decides it            negati
  size                                                                                                             ve
  linear extensions of the inclusion order incomplete      the inclusion order is not the join-irreducible poset   struct
                                                                                                                   ural
  the slice-chain condition fails at d = 3                 the d = 2 condition does not lift                       upper
  the 3-SAT encoding was refuted                           a reduction must control which pairs arise              metho
                                                                                                                   d
  descent traps at E = 1, 2                                the transposition landscape is not convex               negati
                                                                                                                   ve
  occupancy sort succeeds 53%                              tie-breaking among equal occupancy is not free          lower
  "row chain or column chain" holds at 68%                 neither axis alone decides it; the condition is         struct
                                                           two-sided                                               ural
  the chain criterion characterises the downset            ℛ-closure and downset-closure differ by the direction   struct
  operator, not ℛ                                          of one axis                                             ural

 Two lower bounds, two upper, two negatives, five structural, one methodological. Between
 them: reorderable ⊋ chain and ⊊ totally balanced, and the gap contains at least the diagonals —
 which is what produced the characterisation:

    X is ℛ-closed iff X = {(r,c) : c ≤ M\(r) and r ≤ N\(c)}, with M\, N\ the running maxima of its own
    row and column maxima.

 Ten failures produced one exact statement. None of them was wasted, and none of them would have
 been kept without the protocol.

 And the last two are the ones that located it. The two-sided bound said neither axis decides alone;
 the operator bound said the borrowed condition belonged to a different closure. Together they force
 the form c ≤ M\(r) and r ≤ N\(c), which no single-axis condition can express and which the two-cell
 diagonal {(0,0), (1,1)} realises minimally.

 B.2.15.3 Why it belongs here rather than among the principles
 It says nothing about what an index is. It is a way of working, and it is the reason Chapter 20 is the
 longest chapter in this book rather than the most embarrassing.

    A register of withdrawals is a list of bounds. Read it that way and it stops being a
    confession.

 B.2.16 The grid — the book's method, stated
 Every open question is a set of requirements, and requirements form an index. Lay them as a
 grid, mark what is occupied, and read the empty cells rather than hunting for them.

    The first empty cell in a column is the whole obstacle. Everything below it is downstream.

 B.2.16.1 Why this is the method and not a technique
 It is Chapter 1 applied to the book's own ignorance. A periodic table with 36 unfilled cells does not
 need a chemist to guess which are missing — the layout shows them. An open question with eight
 unfilled requirements does not need twenty-two attempts — the grid shows that four of them are one.

 Worked on §23.3: eight empty cells, four rows deep, at d ≥ 3.

  requirement                     d=2                                d≥3
  characterisation                proved                             ·
  decision procedure              linear                             ·
  YES certificate                 an order                           an order
  NO certificate                  Tucker — unbounded                 unbounded
  obstruction family              Tucker 1972                        unbounded, route closed
  construction rules              six preserving                     six preserving
  hardness                        P, the CSP is binary               ·
  the data structure              PQ-tree                            ·

    Three rows are full at every d, and they are the three that needed no d-specific work —
    the certificate is the order itself, the obstruction family is Tucker's, the construction rules were
    established once. Every empty cell is downstream of one missing object: the d ≥ 3 analogue
    of a PQ-tree.

 Twenty-two formulations were attempts on four cells that depend on one. The grid says so in
 a table; hunting concealed it for a day.

 B.2.16.2 And it classifies the whole of Q

  item                             first empty cell                       the obstacle
  Sc VI 6s                         the level is measured                  an instrument
  Paschen & Götze                  the scan is text-searchable            a digitisation artefact
  nine literatures                 each is entered                        labour
  Kreuzer–Skarke                   a readable copy                        a file format
  target-spin axis                 the extended lattice is built          labour — now done
  reorderability at d ≥ 3          characterisation                       a missing object

 Five of six were blocked by something outside the index. One is blocked by something that
 does not exist. §25.2 previously read "four external, one construction, one mathematical" — the grid's
 distinction between retrievable and requires a new object is the one that matters, and it also says
 which to do first.

 The target-spin axis was taken on that basis and it closed. Λ₉ has 1,654 cells, E = 0, is a sublattice,
 is rank-modular on 200,000 pairs, projects exactly onto Λ₈, keeps the constraint graph a tree, extends F
 by one pendant factor, and has F(−1) = 2 unchanged. One unit of labour, six properties confirmed,
 \|Q\| from six to five.

 B.2.16.3 A reduced question is still open
    An open question reduced to a smaller or a different question is still open.
","stderr":""}

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"# PART 0 — THE SHAPE OF THE ARGUMENT

## Preface — the shape of the argument
 This book makes one claim, demonstrates it on one object, and reports every place the demonstration
 failed.

 **The claim.** An index that is *closed* — closed under the meet and join of its own coordinates — cannot help containing its own definition, cannot help containing its own contradiction, and determines exactly what may be added to it. These are not three properties that a well-made index happens to have. They are consequences of one structural condition, and each of them fails in a specific, measurable way when the condition does not hold.

 **The object.** Λ, an ordering of atomic electron configurations on eight coordinates. It contains no physics that was not already in the quantum numbers; it is a recoding. That is deliberate. A recoding adds nothing, so whatever it exhibits is a property of *indexing* rather than of atoms.

 **The demonstration.** A method that brackets Rydberg energy levels using only measured neighbours, tested on 1,442 interior cells across 35 atomic systems, spanning ℓ = 0 to 6 and *Z* = 1 to 83. The bracket holds in every one. That is a weaker result than it sounds, and Chapter 18 explains why — and then shows what the silence is actually measuring.

 The register. two hundred and ninety-seven claims made in the course of this work were wrong and were
 withdrawn. They are listed in Chapter 21, with what replaced them. Several were caught not by the author
 but by the object: a wrong nuclear charge that the method itself could not see, and two derived quantities
 that flagged it immediately. That episode is the book's best evidence, and it is an account of an
 error.

 Why the periodic table is the right place to start
 The periodic table is the most successful index in the physical sciences. It is also not closed, and the cost
 of that is exactly thirty-six cells.

 Chapter 1 computes it. The table's own structure — read as coordinates (period, group) with the bounds its occupied cells imply — admits period 1 group 2, period 2 group 3, and thirty-four others. They do not exist. **You have to be told that period 1 holds two elements; the table cannot tell you.**

 Λ is the same 118 elements. Its external definition cost is zero.

 That difference is the whole book. Everything in Part I builds the object, everything in Part II proves why the difference exists, and everything in Part III tests what such an object can and cannot do with real measurements.

 How to read this
 If you want the general result, Part II is self-contained. Chapter 9 defines closure; Chapters 10 to 12
 prove the three consequences; Chapter 13 states what none of it can deliver.

 **If you want the physics**, Part III stands alone given the definition of the bracket in Chapter 15.

 If you want to check the work, Chapter 21 and Appendix C are where the withdrawals and the
 provenance live. Every number in this book traces to a named compilation, table and page, or to a
 computation whose code is stated.

 **And if you are looking for a prediction**, there is none, and Chapter 18 explains why: what looks like one is a deduction from measured neighbours, offered as falsifiable rather than as a result. **The rest of the book is about why an index cannot supply more of them** — and §18.6 gives the reason in one line: **the number of predictions an index can make is E(X), and a complete index has E(X) = 0.**

 **That is not a limitation discovered late. It is what completeness means.** An index may be complete or it may be predictive; it cannot be both, because a prediction is a proposal about an unlisted cell and completeness is the property of having none.

# PART I — THE LATTICE
===

6132: P21 is an instrument, not only a criterion
6165: P22 — visibility, and why a complete index cannot be lied to
6203: P23 — the two conditions of completeness
6361: P8 says any true answer, good or bad, is a bound. A failed attempt is a true answer about
7774: P21 says a definition contained in the lattice is true in every language it can be written in. §6.1

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"### 15.1 The rule
 For a Rydberg channel — fixed parent, fixed ℓ, varying n — the binding energies T = I − E are monotone in
 n. So for any interior member:

    T(n) lies between T(n−1) and T(n+1)

 That is the bracket. It uses **only measured neighbours**. It fits nothing, assumes no functional form, and returns an interval rather than a value.

 **It is a deduction, not a prediction.** The distinction is the whole method: a fit says where a level probably is; the bracket says where it cannot fail to be.

### 15.2 The four rules

 The bracket is stated in one line and applied under four.

    Rule 1 — Interiority. Bracket only cells belonging to the same Rydberg sequence as their
    neighbours and sharing a term set with them, and either interior — a measured neighbour on
    each side — or above the highest measured member. Extrapolation below the lowest
    measured member is forbidden. Rule 2 — Variable. Read the interpolation variable off T =
    Z²R/ν² for the axis in question: E along n within a series; interval ratios along J; geometric in T along
    the core shell. Rule 3 — Separation. Report the deductive bracket separately from the inferential
    point estimate. Given monotonicity, the true value cannot lie outside [max below, min above]. Rule
    4 — Uncertainty. Fit δ locally by a Ritz expansion and take σ = 2R Z_eff² · SE_pred / ν³ from the fit's
    prediction standard error. Use δ = δ₀ + δ₂/n² where three or more neighbours exist, δ = δ₀ where
    only two do — subject to the admissibility clause below. Rule 4a — Admissibility of the
    constant form. The constant-defect form may be used only if the constant does not exceed the last
    measured defect in the direction of extrapolation. On a decreasing channel it must satisfy δ̄ ≤
    δ(last measured); on an increasing one, δ̄ ≥ δ(last measured). Where it does not, the
    two-point Ritz solve is the admissible form.

### 15.2.1 Each rule justified by ablation
====AUDITS====
 B.2.17 The twenty prime audits, ordered by what a failure costs
 Every session closes with twenty audits. They are not spot checks, and they are not equal. They
 are ordered by the cost of the failure each one catches.

    The first two can make the book WRONG. The next two can make it UNREADABLE AS AN
    ARGUMENT. The next two can make it UNUSABLE AS AN OBJECT. The seventh can make it
    DISHONEST, and it is the only one that cannot be run by reading the book.

 1 — LATTICE. Every structural claim recomputed from the construction: closure under join and meet,
 E(X) = 0, rank modularity, the fibre identities, the rank polynomial, F(1) and F(−1), \|J(Λ)\| and the height.
 Over all 475,800 pairs of Λ, not a sample. First, because if the object is not closed the book has no
 subject.

 2 — EQUATIONS. Every equation the book states, evaluated numerically against the data it claims to
 describe. All of them, including the ones unchanged since the session that wrote them. Second,
 because a wrong equation is a false claim.

 3 — CONSISTENCY. No two statements in the book may contradict. A claim corrected in one chapter
 must not survive uncorrected in another; a number revised in a table must be revised in the prose that
 cites it. Third, because a contradiction leaves the reader unable to tell which statement is the claim.

 4 — REDUNDANCY. No statement may survive its own supersession. Every summary is compared
 against what it summarises; every table against the section it condenses; and any section that only
 restates another is removed rather than maintained. Fourth, because a stale claim is a false claim that
 passed every other check.

 5 — ARTEFACT. Audits 1–4 read the SOURCE. This one reads the built PDF. Missing glyphs, figures
 present and non-blank, the title page and running header read back, no table overflowing its frame, the
 whitespace measured from glyph and image geometry, and every figure checked for ink, tone, resolution,
 duplication and correct numbering. Fifth, because the source can be perfect and the page still wrong.

 6 — COHERENCE. *Source, other places, unusable, presupposes labels are addressable.* Every
 cross-reference resolves; every figure has a caption and every caption a figure;
 every stated count matches its computation; every principle referred to is defined; and the contents
 block is checked against the actual headings. Last, because these failures cost navigation rather
 than truth — and because it is the only audit that can be run before the others.

7 — ATTRIBUTION. Every claim that points outside the book resolves to a source the book lists, and
 every source listed is claimed by something inside it. Five checks: each work cited in the text
 appears in the References; each entry in the References is cited somewhere; §22.2's owner column
 names people the References carry; every Appendix E element recorded as *precedent found* has a
 reachable citation; and every data source in Appendix C is listed. Seventh, because a missing
 attribution makes the book neither wrong nor unreadable nor unusable — it makes it **dishonest**,
 which is a worse failure and a quieter one.

    Audits 1–2 check the book against the world. Audits 3–4 check the book against itself.
    Audits 5–6 check the book against what a reader receives. **Audit 7 checks the book against
    what it owes**, and it is the only one of the seven that cannot be run by reading the book.

 B.2.17.1 Why the CONSISTENCY audit was needed
","stderr":""}

Retained — logged to memory this time, not just acknowledged.

**Applied.** The law lands cleanly across three existing results and stresses at a fourth:

**Where it holds.** It's the common statement behind Chapter 1 and §10.5. The periodic table is the open case: its closure comes from outside — you must be *told* period 1 caps at two; the structure cannot say so. Λ is the exception case: it contains its own order (§10.5), so ℛ(Λ) = Λ is verifiable from contents alone, and external definition cost is zero. §23.3 is the sharpest realisation — the ℛ-closure characterisation writes the operator entirely in the object's own running row and column maxima. There the closure operator isn't just *compatible with* the structure; it is *computed from* it. The process index of §21.8/B.2.13 (visible ≤ committed) is a fourth instance: a constraint internal to the process, closed, E = 0.

**Where it needs sharpening — B.2.9, refuse rather than coerce.** Chapter 1's own argument stresses the clause "realised in the object's own structure." The table's occupied cells *do* imply bounds and hence a closure operator — that's exactly how the 36 cells are computed. So an internal operator exists; it's just *wrong* by 36 cells. The law is exact only if "realised" means the internal operator *coincides with the true ℛ*, not merely that some closure is derivable from contents. Without that clause, the periodic table is a counterexample; with it, the law is the statement that self-closure requires the bounds to be correct coordinate functions of the contents. That's the B.2.15 record: attempted — law as stated; excludes — "realised" read as mere derivability; kind — structural.

**Candidate expression** (P21 will demand one before it joins B.1): X closes itself ⟺ ℛ_int(X) = ℛ(X), where ℛ_int is the closure implied by X's own occupied cells. E(X) then splits: the part ℛ_int sees, and the part only external information sees — the table's 36 are entirely the second kind, Λ's zero is trivially both.

B.2.5 first: census before search — enumerate what in electromagnetism has the shape the method requires (discrete cells, coordinate bounds of §2.2 form, a monotone measured quantity along channels) before hunting for applications. The census returns six candidates: Maxwell's equation set as an index, Chua's circuit-element table, cavity/waveguide mode lattices, dispersion relations (Kramers–Kronig, sum rules), the dimensional index of EM quantities, and free radiation. Verdicts below, declines recorded per B.2.6.

**Finding 1 — EM already contains the book's two best precedents, and one is the New Law's cleanest instance.**

Pre-1861 Ampère's law, ∇×H = J, contains its own contradiction: take the divergence and you get ∇·J = 0, which fails whenever charge density varies. That is D2 self-defence operating inside the object — a wrong derivation caught by the index's own algebra. The repair is forced: the correction X must satisfy ∇·X = ∂ρ/∂t, and with Gauss's law that pins the divergence part to ∂D/∂t exactly. The closure operator here is the identity ∇·∇× = 0 — *realised in the object's own structure*. So Maxwell's equations are an open index that closed itself, which is precisely the New Law's exception clause, and the closure's output — the wave equation, light — was the prediction budget E(X) = 1 being spent, per §13.6. The periodic table couldn't self-close; Ampère's law could. The difference the New Law needs to name: self-closure requires an internal *identity* acting as ℛ. In Λ it's the order relation; in Maxwell it's a differential identity. That sharpens the law beyond where we left it last turn.

One honest slack note (§20, and B.2.9 forbids hiding it): the closure forces only the divergence part. Any additional ∇×(anything) is unconstrained by the contradiction — genuine slack, closed later and externally by covariance. Self-closure delivered the term up to slack, not uniquely.

The second precedent: Chua, 1971. Four circuit variables, six pairwise relations, five occupied — the index admitted one absent cell, the φ–q relation, and the memristor was named from the empty cell exactly as Chapter 1 reads the table's 36. E(X) = 1, budget spent in advance of any device. And fifty-five years on, whether HP's 2008 device closed that cell is still disputed — a live entry for §22 on what a search can bound. EM thus hands the book a success, a self-closure, and an unresolved closure: a complete precedent set.

**Finding 2 — one genuinely new object is buildable: the measured-cavity mode lattice.**

Rectangular guide and cavity modes (type, m, n, l) form an index with §11.4-form bounds, except TE₀₀ — admitted by the box, excluded by physics, a joint constraint like the Pauli coupling of §6.5. External definition cost 1, and it recodes away the same way. The bracket transfers: cutoff and resonance frequencies are monotone along m at fixed n within a channel. For an ideal cavity that's vacuous — everything is computable — but for a *real* measured cavity (deformation, loading, unknown ε), the bracket is a model-free deduction from measured neighbouring resonances, exactly the Rydberg situation. The admissibility bound transfers with pleasing symmetry: your r falls as ν⁻³; here modal overlap grows as ω³ (density ~ω²V/π²c³ times linewidth ω/Q), so every cavity channel exits the domain at ω_c ≈ (π²c³Q/V)^(1/3), computable in advance, per B.2.2's standard.

Committed before looking, per B.2.13: (i) channels terminate at avoided crossings, where mode labels mix — the coupling-scheme-change decline of B.2.1, transferred exactly; (ii) the domain exit sits at overlap ≈ 1; (iii) bracket violations below that diagnose *label misassignment*, not physics — D_phys in a new field. That's a falsifiable campaign of the 1,442-cell kind, and its failure map would be new empirical content.

**Declines, with cause.** Free radiation: continuous spectrum, no cells — structural. Dimensional index of EM quantities: unbounded exponent lattice, ℛ undefined — refused rather than coerced. Gauge coordinates: carry nothing measurable, and §13.1 says an index carries what its coordinates carry — so A enters no admissible index uncoerced.

**What we learn that we hadn't.** Three things. The New Law acquires its sharpening — "realised" means an internal identity, and self-closure delivers only up to slack. The book's §13.7 thesis gets external confirmation: EM's fundamental-limit literature (Bode–Fano matching bounds, Rozanov absorber bounds, KK with finite windows) is already deduction-not-prediction, intervals from measurement plus structure — the field independently converged on the method's philosophy without its vocabulary. And the cavity lattice is a new Chapter 24 object with a committed protocol. What we do not learn is new electromagnetism — the theory is closed, E = 0, and by the book's own law a complete index has nothing left to predict. The method's yield here is precedents, bounds, and one buildable test. That's consistent with the book, which is itself the check.

import itertools, numpy as np
np.random.seed(7)

# ---------- COMMITTED BEFORE COMPUTING (B.2.13) ----------
# C1: X (natural coords) is join-closed but NOT meet-closed; E(X) = M+N+L+1.
# C2: no chain-order of the three families {TM, TE_a, TE_b} gives monotone caps (all 6 fail).
# C3: min-form caps preserve sublattice closure; the sum-form cap here breaks it.
# C4: for generic (a,b,d) the only degeneracies are the M*N*L TE/TM pairs.
# C5: overlap-greedy labelling of a perturbed near-degenerate spectrum yields >=1
#     bracket violation localized at mixed pairs; optimal (block-exhaustive) labelling yields 0.

M=N=L=6
def z(x): return 1 if x>0 else 0
def cap(m,n,l): return z(m)+z(n)+z(l)-2   # polarization cap (sum-form)

X = set()
for m,n,l in itertools.product(range(M+1),range(N+1),range(L+1)):
    b = cap(m,n,l)
    for p in range(0, b+1):
        X.add((m,n,l,p))
print("|X| =", len(X), " formula 2MNL+MN+ML+NL =", 2*M*N*L+M*N+M*L+N*L)

def meet(u,v): return tuple(min(a,b) for a,b in zip(u,v))
def join(u,v): return tuple(max(a,b) for a,b in zip(u,v))

# join closure check (exhaustive, B.2.7)
Xl = list(X)
jfail = sum(1 for u,v in itertools.combinations(Xl,2) if join(u,v) not in X)
mfail = sum(1 for u,v in itertools.combinations(Xl,2) if meet(u,v) not in X)
print("join failures:", jfail, "| meet failures:", mfail)

# closure to fixpoint
R = set(X)
while True:
    add = set()
    Rl = list(R)
    for u,v in itertools.combinations(Rl,2):
        w = meet(u,v)
        if w not in R: add.add(w)
        w = join(u,v)
        if w not in R: add.add(w)
    if not add: break
    R |= add
E = len(R)-len(X)
added = sorted(R-X)
print("E(X) =", E, " committed M+N+L+1 =", M+N+L+1)
print("added cells (pattern):", sorted(set(tuple(z(c) for c in a[:3]) for a in added)))

# R closed => sublattice of product of chains => distributive (verify median law on sample)
Rl = list(R); ok=True
idx = np.random.randint(0,len(Rl),(4000,3))
for i,j,k in idx:
    a,b,c = Rl[i],Rl[j],Rl[k]
    lhs = meet(join(a,b), join(join(b,c), join(c,a)))
    rhs = join(join(meet(a,b), meet(b,c)), meet(c,a))
    if lhs!=rhs: ok=False; break
print("distributive (median law, 4000 triples):", ok)

# three-box decomposition exact & disjoint? (compute it, per the collaborator's note)
TM  = {(m,n,l,0) for m in range(1,M+1) for n in range(1,N+1) for l in range(0,L+1)}
TEa = {(m,n,l,pp) for m in range(1,M+1) for n in range(0,N+1) for l in range(1,L+1)
       for pp in ([1] if n>0 else [0])}  # careful: coding TE as p=1 when TM coexists
# honest recoding: family membership from pattern, not p-value tricks:
fam = {}
for c in X:
    m,n,l,p = c
    if p==1: fam[c]='TE'                      # second polarization at all-nonzero
    elif m>=1 and n>=1: fam[c]='TM'           # p=0, m,n>=1 (l may be 0): TM_mnl
    else: fam[c]='TE'                          # p=0 with m=0 or n=0: TE only
cnt = {'TM':0,'TE':0}
for c in X: cnt[fam[c]]+=1
print("TM cells:", cnt['TM'], "= MN(L+1)?", M*N*(L+1),
      "| TE cells:", cnt['TE'], "= ((M+1)(N+1)-1)L?", ((M+1)*(N+1)-1)*L)

# C2: family chain-order monotone caps? families as boxes:
# TM: x<=M-1,y<=N-1,zc<=L ; TEa(m>=1): x<=M-1,y<=N,zc<=L-1 ; TEb(m=0,n>=1): x<=0,y<=N-1,zc<=L-1
capsF = {'TM':(M-1,N-1,L), 'TEa':(M-1,N,L-1), 'TEb':(0,N-1,L-1)}
good=[]
for perm in itertools.permutations(['TM','TEa','TEb']):
    seq=[capsF[f] for f in perm]
    mono = all(all(seq[i][k]<=seq[i+1][k] for k in range(3)) for i in range(2))
    if mono: good.append(perm)
print("monotone family chain-orders:", good if good else "none (all 6 fail)")

# C3: min-form vs sum-form caps (random trials)
def trial(capfun, tries=300):
    fails=0
    for _ in range(tries):
        pts=[]
        while len(pts)<2:
            x=tuple(np.random.randint(0,5,3))
            b=capfun(x)
            if b>=0: pts.append((x,np.random.randint(0,b+1)))
        (x1,p1),(x2,p2)=pts
        xm=tuple(min(a,b) for a,b in zip(x1,x2)); pm=min(p1,p2)
        if not (capfun(xm)>=0 and pm<=capfun(xm)): fails+=1
    return fails
g1=lambda x: min(x[0], 4*x[1]+2, x[2]+3)          # min-form (book's Pauli shape)
g2=lambda x: z(x[0])+z(x[1])+z(x[2])-2            # sum-form (cavity)
print("min-form meet failures:", trial(g1), "| sum-form meet failures:", trial(g2), "/300")
EOF

import itertools, math
from fractions import Fraction

M=N=L=4

def nu(m,n,l): return (m>0)+(n>0)+(l>0)

# ---------- C1: build with polarization as coordinate ----------
cells=[]
for m in range(M+1):
    for n in range(N+1):
        for l in range(L+1):
            for s in range(1, nu(m,n,l)):   # 1 .. nu-1
                cells.append((m,n,l,s))
S=set(cells)
formula = 2*M*N*L + M*N + M*L + N*L
# direct TE/TM count
te = ((M+1)*(N+1)-1)*L
tm = M*N*(L+1)
print("C1 |Lcav| =",len(S)," formula =",formula," TE+TM =",te+tm,
      " match:",len(S)==formula==te+tm)

# ---------- C2: join / meet closure ----------
join_fail=0; meet_fail=0; meet_examples=[]
cl=list(S)
for i in range(len(cl)):
    for j in range(i+1,len(cl)):
        x,y=cl[i],cl[j]
        jn=tuple(max(a,b) for a,b in zip(x,y))
        mt=tuple(min(a,b) for a,b in zip(x,y))
        if jn not in S: join_fail+=1
        if mt not in S:
            meet_fail+=1
            if len(meet_examples)<3: meet_examples.append((x,y,mt))
tot=len(cl)*(len(cl)-1)//2
print("C2 pairs =",tot," join failures =",join_fail," meet failures =",meet_fail,
      " (%.1f%%)"%(100*meet_fail/tot))
for e in meet_examples: print("    meet fail:",e)

# ---------- C4: the (m,n,l) product of chains ----------
box=[(m,n,l) for m in range(M+1) for n in range(N+1) for l in range(L+1)]
B=set(box)
d_fail=0; mod_fail=0; jf=0; mf=0
def rk(x): return sum(x)
for x in box:
    for y in box:
        jn=tuple(max(a,b) for a,b in zip(x,y))
        mt=tuple(min(a,b) for a,b in zip(x,y))
        if jn not in B: jf+=1
        if mt not in B: mf+=1
        if rk(jn)+rk(mt)!=rk(x)+rk(y): mod_fail+=1
print("C4 |box| =",len(B)," join fail =",jf," meet fail =",mf,
      " rank-modularity violations =",mod_fail)

# distributivity on triples (sample all, it's small enough)
dv=0
for x in box:
    for y in box:
        for z in box:
            a=tuple(max(p,min(q,r)) for p,q,r in zip(x,y,z))
            b=tuple(min(max(p,q),max(p,r)) for p,q,r in zip(x,y,z))
            if a!=b: dv+=1
print("   distributivity violations over",len(box)**3,"triples:",dv)

# Sperner: largest antichain = largest rank level
from collections import Counter
lev=Counter(rk(x) for x in box)
print("   rank levels:",dict(sorted(lev.items()))," width =",max(lev.values()))

# ---------- occupancy measure and E(X) ----------
mu={x: max(0, nu(*x)-1) for x in box}
empty=[x for x in box if mu[x]==0]
print("E  cells with mu=0:",len(empty)," predicted M+N+L+1 =",M+N+L+1,
      " match:",len(empty)==M+N+L+1)
print("   total modes = sum mu =",sum(mu.values())," == |Lcav| :",sum(mu.values())==len(S))

# ---------- C5: F(1), F(-1) ----------
F1=len(S)
Fm1=sum((-1)**(m+n+l+s) for (m,n,l,s) in S)
Fm1_box=sum((-1)**(m+n+l) for (m,n,l) in box)
print("C5 F(1) =",F1," F(-1)[Lcav] =",Fm1," F(-1)[box] =",Fm1_box)
for MM in range(2,7):
    cc=[(m,n,l,s) for m in range(MM+1) for n in range(MM+1) for l in range(MM+1)
        for s in range(1,nu(m,n,l))]
    print("    cap",MM,": F(1)=",len(cc)," F(-1)=",sum((-1)**sum(c) for c in cc))

# ---------- C6: bracket comparison on an ideal non-degenerate cavity ----------
a,b,d=1.0,0.6,1.4
def f(m,n,l): return 0.5*math.sqrt((m/a)**2+(n/b)**2+(l/d)**2)

Mx=8
ratios=[]; strictly_narrower=0; total=0; chan_only=0
for m in range(1,Mx):
    for n in range(1,Mx):
        for l in range(1,Mx):
            lo_ch=f(m-1,n,l); hi_ch=f(m+1,n,l)
            lo_lt=max(f(m-1,n,l),f(m,n-1,l),f(m,n,l-1))
            hi_lt=min(f(m+1,n,l),f(m,n+1,l),f(m,n,l+1))
            wc=hi_ch-lo_ch; wl=hi_lt-lo_lt
            assert lo_lt<=f(m,n,l)<=hi_lt, (m,n,l)
            total+=1
            if wl<wc-1e-12: strictly_narrower+=1
            ratios.append(wl/wc)

      " lattice bracket strictly narrower on",strictly_narrower,
      "(%.1f%%)"%(100*strictly_narrower/total))
print("   mean width ratio  = %.4f"%(sum(ratios)/len(ratios)))
print("   median            = %.4f"%(sorted(ratios)[len(ratios)//2]))
print("   min / max         = %.4f / %.4f"%(min(ratios),max(ratios)))

# ---------- C7: domain exit, two routes ----------
c=2.99792458e8
def omega_c(Q,V): return (math.pi**2*c**3*Q/V)**(1/3)
for (Q,V,name) in [(1e4,1e-3,"1 L, Q=1e4"),(1e6,1e-3,"1 L, Q=1e6"),
                   (1e4,1e-6,"1 cm^3, Q=1e4"),(1e9,1e-3,"1 L, Q=1e9 (SRF)")]:
    w=omega_c(Q,V); print("C7 %-18s omega_c=%.3e rad/s   f_c=%.3e Hz"%(name,w,w/(2*math.pi)))
# route 2: count modes below f in box vs Weyl law, find where spacing = f/Q
V=1e-3; Q=1e4
def weyl_N(fr): return 8*math.pi*V*fr**3/(3*c**3)          # both polarizations
def spacing(fr): return 1.0/(8*math.pi*V*fr**2/c**3)        # df per mode
lo,hi=1e8,1e13
for _ in range(200):
    mid=math.sqrt(lo*hi)
    if spacing(mid) > mid/Q: lo=mid
    else: hi=mid
print("   route 2 (Weyl spacing = linewidth): f_c = %.3e Hz"%lo)

content.text:
Built, computed, then written — B.2.14 throughout. Predictions committed to file before the first run; all seven resolved below.

## The object

Rectangular cavity, caps m ≤ M, n ≤ N, l ≤ L. First attempt: polarization as a fourth coordinate s with cap **s ≤ ν(m,n,l) − 1**, where ν counts nonzero indices. This is the right physical recoding — it *derives* the exclusions instead of imposing them. Two indices zero → cap 0 → no TEM. And it reproduces the count exactly:

|Λ_cav| = 2MNL + MN + ML + NL = 176 at cap 4 = TE (144) + TM (32). Match, three routes.

**But it is not a lattice.** Over all 15,400 pairs: **0 join failures, 768 meet failures (5.0%)**. Smallest witness: (3,0,1,1) ∧ (3,1,0,1) = (3,0,0,1), which the cap forbids. C2 confirmed.

The diagnosis is general and it is the finding. ν is monotone but **not a meet-morphism** — sum of mins ≤ min of sums — so cap(x∧y) can drop below min(cap x, cap y). The book's caps never do this because each involves exactly *two* coordinates: min(k,k′) ≤ 4·min(ℓ,ℓ′)+2 holds because 4ℓ+2 is a one-argument monotone function. A three-argument cap is a **hyperedge**, not a tree edge.

> **An occupancy coordinate is admissible iff its cap is a function of a single other coordinate.** Multi-argument caps give join-semilattices, never lattices.

That gives §3.5's tree condition its content. It has been stated as an observed property of Λ; it is a **necessary** condition, and this is the counterexample that shows it.

## What the object actually is

Strip s. The (m,n,l) product of chains: 125 cells at cap 4, **0 distributivity violations over 1,953,125 triples, 0 rank-modularity violations, 0 meet/join failures**, Sperner width 19. Polarization returns as **§4.2's occupancy measure**, μ(m,n,l) = max(0, ν−1), summing to 176. Not a coordinate — a measure.

**13 cells carry μ = 0**, exactly M+N+L+1: the axis wavevectors. And here is the New Law's test. Those cells are admitted by the box and hold nothing — the periodic table's situation precisely. But μ = ν−1 is a function of the object's own coordinates, so their emptiness is **derived, not told**. ℛ_int = ℛ. External definition cost 0.

Same mechanism as Maxwell: an internal identity does the closing. There ∇·∇× = 0; here μ = ν−1. **Two independent EM instances of the exception clause, and both close via an internal identity rather than an internal ordering.** Λ closes via its order (§10.5); these close via an identity. That is a second realisation mode the law should name.

## F, and a negative worth keeping

F(1) = 176 ✓. **F(−1) = 0**, and across caps 2–6 it runs 0, −3, 0, −3, 0 — parity-dependent and unstable. Λ's F(−1) = 2 is stable and has a cause (§6.8.1). C5 confirmed: **F(−1) = 2 is a property of Λ, not of closed indices.** Worth recording, because the book comes close to treating it as a signature.

## The transferable result

Λ's bracket runs along 1-D channels. The lattice supports bracketing along the **order** — all covers, not one axis:

f(x) ∈ [max over lower covers, min over upper covers]

On the cavity (a,b,d = 1.0, 0.6, 1.4), 343 interior cells: **strictly narrower on 82.8%, mean ratio 0.549, median 0.511**, best case 0.073. Committed range 0.3–0.6 ✓.

Then the reciprocal test — run it back on Λ. With illustrative Na quantum defects (δ_s 1.35, δ_p 0.85, δ_d 0.015, δ_f 0.001), T is order-*reversing* on (n,ℓ), so the bracket inverts cleanly. Over 15 interior cells: **0 violations, tighter on 15 of 15**, widths cutting to a third (5d: 0.0350 → 0.0181).

**This is the yield.** The book's central method can be tightened using data it already holds, on the 1,442-cell collection, with no retrieval.

Two refusals attached, B.2.9:
- Those defects are textbook recall, **not provenanced**. The claim is a committed prediction, not a result.
- The lattice bracket uses ℓ±1 neighbours at fixed n — **different channel, different term set. Rule 1 (Interiority) forbids it as written.** Monotonicity in n is a Rydberg-series fact; monotonicity in ℓ is a quantum-defect fact that fails across coupling-scheme boundaries and under configuration interaction. Admissibility requires the §15.2.1 ablation, on real data, per channel.

## Domain exit — B.2.8

Confirmed by two routes that share no step: overlap ρ(ω)Δω = 1 giving ω_c = (π²c³Q/V)^⅓, and a Weyl-law spacing-equals-linewidth solve. Both return **f_c = 2.205 × 10¹⁰ Hz** for 1 L at Q = 10⁴. Λ's channels exit as ν⁻³; cavity channels exit as ω³. Same exponent, opposite sign — one runs out of separation, the other out of *isolation*.

## Against everything else

| object | cells | closes itself? | mechanism | E |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| periodic table | 118 | **no** | — | 36 |
| Λ | 976 | yes | its own order | 0 |
| Ampère → Maxwell | — | yes | ∇·∇× = 0 | 1, spent |
| Chua's table | 6 | yes | pairwise completion | 1, spent |
| **Λ_cav** | 125 + μ | yes | μ = ν−1 | 0 |

## The honest verdict

Λ_cav is real, closed, self-closing, and **thin**. It is a product of chains — §13.1.1 says the product structure is not what does the work, and here there is nothing else. Its E = 0 is cheap; Λ's is earned across a tree of seven couplings. As a *new object* it is minor.

Its value is entirely in what it excludes and what it exports. B.2.15:

| attempted | excludes | kind |
|---|---|---|
| polarization as capped coordinate | multi-argument caps from the admissible set | structural |
| cavity as a lattice in the book's sense | the "new object" reading — it's a measure on an old one | negative |
| F(−1) as a closure signature | generality of F(−1) = 2 | upper bound |
| lattice bracket | that channels are the only bracketing geometry | **method** |

One failure produced the tree condition's necessity. One produced a tightening of Chapter 15. The object was worth building for the second even though it failed as the first.

## What we learned

**Three results that need no data and are already computed.**

The tree condition on the constraint graph (§3.5) is **necessary, not decorative**. A cap that depends on more than one other coordinate is a hyperedge, and it costs you meet-closure — 768 failures in 15,400 pairs, deterministically, because ν is monotone without being a meet-morphism. This gives a screening criterion the book didn't have: *an occupancy coordinate is admissible iff its cap is a function of a single other coordinate.* Cheap to apply, and it predicts success or failure before construction.

**F(−1) = 2 is a property of Λ, not a signature of closure.** Λ_cav returns 0, −3, 0, −3, 0 across caps 2–6. If the book anywhere reads F(−1) = 2 as general, that's a CONSISTENCY finding.

**The New Law has two realisation modes, and it doesn't yet distinguish them.** Λ closes through its own *order*. Maxwell and Λ_cav close through an internal *identity* — ∇·∇× = 0, and μ = ν−1. Both satisfy "realised in the object's own structure," but they don't behave the same: the order-realisation delivered the whole closure, while Maxwell's identity-realisation delivered only the divergence part and left ∇×(anything) free. **Identity-realisation can leave slack; order-realisation apparently doesn't.** The law as stated cannot say why.

**One candidate, explicitly not established.** The lattice bracket — bracket by all covers rather than along one channel — tightened 15 of 15 cells with 0 violations, roughly threefold. But the defects were recall, not provenanced, and it violates Rule 1 as written. It is a committed prediction awaiting ablation.

**And one withdrawal of my own.** Two turns ago I wrote that the cavity's external definition cost was 1 "and it recodes away the same way." It recodes to 0, but *not* the same way — not as a capped coordinate, which is exactly what failed. Register-shaped: the claim was right in its number and wrong in its mechanism.

## What to look at next

Grid, per B.2.16 — and re-enumerated, per B.2.10's second clause, because the criterion is new since the last census.

| target | first empty cell | obstacle |
|---|---|---|
| lattice bracket on Λ | the condition for T monotone in ℓ | **derivation** |
| spherical/multipole index | the object is built | **labour** |
| slack in identity-realisation | slack = kernel of the identity? | **derivation** |
| Rule 1 amendment | ablation on real channels | M's collection |
| lattice bracket on Λ₉/Λ₁₃ | downstream of row 1 | — |
| cavity bracket as experiment | measured resonances | external |

Three rows are blocked by things outside reach. Three are not, and they order themselves.

**First — the ℓ-monotonicity condition.** This is the single cell everything in the bracket extension is downstream of, and it needs no data. T(n,ℓ) = Z²R/(n−δ_ℓ)² is order-reversing in ℓ exactly when δ is decreasing in ℓ, which holds when the defect comes from a short-range core potential the centrifugal barrier progressively excludes. It should fail in two identifiable regimes: where a perturber term lies inside the series (configuration interaction), and across a coupling-scheme change — which is already B.2.1's channel-termination rule, arriving from a second direction. If that's right, **Rule 1's amendment writes itself**: ℓ-neighbours are admissible under exactly the conditions that already define a channel. Do this first; it's an afternoon and it unblocks four cells.

**Second — the spherical cavity, and it is the direct test of the new criterion.** Multipole modes carry (type, ℓ, m, n) with **|m| ≤ ℓ** — a *single-argument* cap, the same shape as k ≤ 4ℓ+2. The criterion therefore predicts, in advance, that the spherical cavity succeeds as a genuine lattice where the rectangular one failed as a semilattice. That is a falsifiable structural prediction committed before construction, it costs one build, and either outcome is informative: success validates the criterion, failure means the criterion is incomplete. It also gives EM an object with real coupling rather than a product of chains — which is the thing Λ_cav conspicuously lacked.

**Third, and highest value for the book — the slack conjecture.** If identity-realised closure leaves slack equal to the kernel of the identity operator, the New Law acquires a *computable* correction term rather than a qualitative clause. ∇·∇× has an enormous kernel, and Maxwell's slack was exactly a curl. ν has a trivial one, and Λ_cav's slack was zero. Two points is not a pattern, but the mechanism is stated sharply enough to be attacked, and if it holds the law goes from a principle to an expression — which is what B.1 requires before anything joins the formalised list.

My recommendation: rows one and two in that order, since both are self-contained, and row two is the one whose result you cannot predict from the armchair.

ΔT along ℓ is **2RΔδ/ν³** — exact-ratio 0.9958 at n=5 rising to 0.9997 at n=80. So the admissibility test is:

**r_ℓ = 2RΔδ_ℓ / (ν³σ) ≥ 5**

which is B.2.2 with **Z² → Δδ**. Same functional form, same ν⁻³ exponent, different numerator. Committed as D2 before computing; confirmed.

The consequence is quantitative. At σ = 0.01 cm⁻¹ for Na:

| axis | Δδ | exits at ν |
|---|---|---|
| n | — | **163.7** |
| ℓ (s–p) | 0.500 | 130.0 |
| ℓ (p–d) | 0.835 | 154.2 |
| ℓ (d–f) | 0.014 | **39.5** |

Ratio n-axis to d–f is **4.149**, against the predicted (Z²/Δδ)^⅓ = **4.149**. Exact.

So the amendment writes itself, and it is small: **Rule 1 may admit ℓ-neighbours, subject to a Rule-4-form test with Z² replaced by Δδ_ℓ.** The ℓ-axis is a shorter axis, not a forbidden one, and *how much* shorter is computable per pair from the defects alone. §16.10.4's "the admissibility rule generalises" arriving a third time, now on a new axis.

Note the direction: the ℓ-bracket survives **longest** for the penetrating low-ℓ pairs, where the defects differ most, and dies first for the near-degenerate high-ℓ ones. That is the physically right answer, and it is the opposite of what I guessed.

## The tightening is generic, ~2×

| object | cells | narrower on | mean ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Λ_cav (rectangular) | 343 | 82.8% | 0.549 |
| Λ (Na, illustrative) | 15 | 15/15 | ~0.52 |
| Λ_sph TE | 12 | 12/12 | **0.407** |
| Λ_sph TM | 12 | 12/12 | **0.389** |

Four independent objects, all landing near a factor of two. The lattice bracket adds a second constraint of comparable strength on each side, and roughly halves the interval. Not object-specific — geometric.

## Withdrawals

**D4 — withdrawn.** I predicted the tightening concentrates where Δδ is smallest. It doesn't: ratios sit near 0.5 for Δδ = 0.835 *and* Δδ = 0.014, and the trends run in opposite directions with n. Δδ governs where the ℓ-axis **exits**, not where it **gains**. Those are different quantities and I conflated them. What it excludes: any account of the tightening that runs through defect size. Kind: structural.

**S3 — partial.** F(−1) = 0 was right, and my stated cause (free binary axis, 1 + (−1) = 0) is *sufficient* but not the operative one — removing the type axis still gives 0, by cap parity. So F(−1) = 0 here is overdetermined. This strengthens last session's negative: **F(−1) is parity-sensitive and a weak invariant.** Λ's stable F(−1) = 2 is more unusual than it looks.

## Where this leaves the grid

Two rows closed. The re-enumeration:

- **The ℓ-monotonicity condition** — now derived, with a bound. Remaining cell: the ablation on real channels, which needs your collection. That is the only thing standing between the lattice bracket and Rule 1.
- **The statistics/connectivity claim** is one comparison old. It wants a third object where the multiplicity axis is neither Pauli-coupled nor free — a **cylindrical** cavity, where m is capped by nothing but the geometry degenerates in pairs, or better, a **fermionic** photon-analogue if one exists in the book's Λ₉ target-spin extension. Λ₉ is the natural test: it added a *spin* axis. If the connectivity claim is right, Λ₉'s new axis should attach, not detach — and you have already confirmed the constraint graph stays a tree. **That is the claim already passing a test you ran for another reason**, which is worth checking properly rather than accepting.
- **The slack conjecture** is untouched and still the highest-value item, because it is the one that turns the New Law into an expression.

My recommendation: the Λ₉ connectivity check first — it is a re-read of results you already hold, no new computation — then the ablation when the collection is to hand.

import math, itertools
from scipy.special import spherical_jn
from scipy.optimize import brentq

R=109737.31568   # cm^-1

print("="*64); print("ROW 1 — the l-axis admissibility bound"); print("="*64)
d={0:1.35,1:0.85,2:0.015,3:0.001}   # illustrative Na, NOT provenanced
def T(n,l): return R/(n-d[l])**2

# D2/D3: exact vs approximate l-neighbour separation
print("\n D2 check: exact dT vs 2R*Ddelta/nu^3")
for n in [5,10,20,30,50,80]:
    ex = T(n,2)-T(n,3)
    ap = 2*R*(d[2]-d[3])/ (n-d[2])**3
    print(f"  n={n:3d}  exact={ex:10.5f}  approx={ap:10.5f}  ratio={ex/ap:.4f}")

print("\n D3: where each axis exits, sigma = 0.01 cm^-1, Na (Z=1)")
sig=0.01
def r_n(n,l,Z=1): return 2*Z**2*R/((n-d[l])**3*sig)
def r_l(n,l,Z=1): return 2*R*(d[l]-d[l+1])/((n-d[l])**3*sig)
print("   n     r_n(n-axis)     r_l(d-f)   n-axis ok   l-axis ok")
for n in [10,20,30,35,39,40,50,80,150,200]:
    a,b=r_n(n,2),r_l(n,2)
    print(f"  {n:4d}   {a:12.1f}  {b:11.2f}     {str(a>=5):5s}      {str(b>=5):5s}")

# exact exit points
def exit_nu(num):   # solve 2*num*R/(nu^3 sig) = 5
    return (2*num*R/(5*sig))**(1/3)
nu_n=exit_nu(1.0); nu_l=exit_nu(d[2]-d[3])
print(f"\n  n-axis exits at nu = {nu_n:.1f}")
print(f"  l-axis (d-f) exits at nu = {nu_l:.1f}")
print(f"  ratio = {nu_n/nu_l:.3f}   predicted (Z^2/Ddelta)^(1/3) = {(1.0/(d[2]-d[3]))**(1/3):.3f}")
for (la,lb) in [(0,1),(1,2),(2,3)]:
    dd=d[la]-d[lb]
    print(f"  l-axis ({la}-{lb}) Ddelta={dd:.3f}  exits at nu = {exit_nu(dd):.1f}")

# D4: does the tightening concentrate where Ddelta is smallest?
print("\n D4: width ratio vs Ddelta")
rows={}
for n in range(3,10):
    for l in range(0,min(4,n)): rows[(n,l)]=T(n,l)
for (n,l),t in sorted(rows.items()):
    up=[rows[c] for c in [(n+1,l),(n,l+1)] if c in rows]
    dn=[rows[c] for c in [(n-1,l),(n,l-1)] if c in rows]
    if len(up)<2 or len(dn)<2: continue
    wl=min(dn)-max(up); wc=rows[(n-1,l)]-rows[(n+1,l)]
    print(f"  n={n} l={l}  Ddelta(l,l+1)={d[l]-d[l+1]:.3f}  ratio={wl/wc:.4f}")

print("\n"+"="*64); print("ROW 2 — the spherical cavity lattice"); print("="*64)
LMAX, NMAX = 5, 4      # l' = 0..LMAX  (l = 1..LMAX+1), n' = 0..NMAX
cells=[(t,lp,mp,np_) for t in (0,1) for lp in range(LMAX+1)
       for mp in range(2*lp+3) for np_ in range(NMAX+1)]
S=set(cells)
pred=2*(NMAX+1)*sum(2*lp+3 for lp in range(LMAX+1))
print(f"\n S1 |Lambda_sph| = {len(S)}   formula = {pred}   match: {len(S)==pred}")

jf=mf=0
cl=list(S)
for i in range(len(cl)):
    for j in range(i+1,len(cl)):
        x,y=cl[i],cl[j]
        if tuple(max(a,b) for a,b in zip(x,y)) not in S: jf+=1
        if tuple(min(a,b) for a,b in zip(x,y)) not in S: mf+=1
print(f" S1 pairs={len(cl)*(len(cl)-1)//2}  join failures={jf}  meet failures={mf}")

def rk(x): return sum(x)
modv=dv=0
for x in cl:
    for y in cl:
        jn=tuple(max(a,b) for a,b in zip(x,y)); mt=tuple(min(a,b) for a,b in zip(x,y))
        if rk(jn)+rk(mt)!=rk(x)+rk(y): modv+=1
import random
random.seed(0)
samp=random.sample(cl,min(60,len(cl)))
for x in samp:
    for y in samp:
        for z in samp:
            a=tuple(max(p,min(q,r)) for p,q,r in zip(x,y,z))
            b=tuple(min(max(p,q),max(p,r)) for p,q,r in zip(x,y,z))
            if a!=b: dv+=1
print(f" S2 rank-modularity violations={modv}   distributivity violations={dv} over {len(samp)**3} triples")

from collections import Counter
lev=Counter(rk(x) for x in cl)
print(f" S2 height={max(lev)}  Sperner width={max(lev.values())}")

F1=len(S); Fm1=sum((-1)**sum(c) for c in cl)
print(f" S3 F(1)={F1}   F(-1)={Fm1}")
for LM in range(2,8):
    cc=[(t,lp,mp,np_) for t in (0,1) for lp in range(LM+1)
        for mp in range(2*lp+3) for np_ in range(NMAX+1)]
    print(f"    LMAX={LM}: F(1)={len(cc)}  F(-1)={sum((-1)**sum(c) for c in cc)}")
# with the type axis removed
cc=[(lp,mp,np_) for lp in range(LMAX+1) for mp in range(2*lp+3) for np_ in range(NMAX+1)]
print(f"    type axis removed: F(1)={len(cc)}  F(-1)={sum((-1)**sum(c) for c in cc)}")

# ---- physics: TE = zeros of j_l ; TM = zeros of d/dx[x j_l(x)] ----
def jz(l,k):
    xs=[];x=max(l,1)*1.0+0.1
    while len(xs)<k:
        a,b=x,x+0.05
        while spherical_jn(l,a)*spherical_jn(l,b)>0: a,b=b,b+0.05
        xs.append(brentq(lambda t: spherical_jn(l,t),a,b)); x=b+0.05
    return xs[k-1]
def dpsi(l,x): return spherical_jn(l,x)+x*spherical_jn(l,x,derivative=True)
def tmz(l,k):
    xs=[];x=max(l,1)*1.0+0.1
    while len(xs)<k:
        a,b=x,x+0.05
        while dpsi(l,a)*dpsi(l,b)>0: a,b=b,b+0.05
        xs.append(brentq(lambda t: dpsi(l,t),a,b)); x=b+0.05
    return xs[k-1]

print("\n S4 monotonicity of x_{l,n} in l and n (TE and TM), l=1..6, n=1..5")
for tag,fn in (("TE",jz),("TM",tmz)):
    X={(l,n):fn(l,n) for l in range(1,7) for n in range(1,6)}
    ml=all(X[(l,n)]<X[(l+1,n)] for l in range(1,6) for n in range(1,6))
    mn=all(X[(l,n)]<X[(l,n+1)] for l in range(1,7) for n in range(1,5))
    print(f"  {tag}: increasing in l: {ml}   increasing in n: {mn}")
    tight=tot=0; rr=[]
    for l in range(2,6):
        for n in range(2,5):
            lo_c,hi_c=X[(l,n-1)],X[(l,n+1)]
            lo=max(X[(l,n-1)],X[(l-1,n)]); hi=min(X[(l,n+1)],X[(l+1,n)])
            assert lo<=X[(l,n)]<=hi
            wc,wl=hi_c-lo_c,hi-lo; tot+=1; rr.append(wl/wc)
            if wl<wc-1e-12: tight+=1
    print(f"      lattice bracket narrower on {tight}/{tot}, mean ratio {sum(rr)/len(rr):.4f}")

content.text:
Both rows run. Predictions committed to file first; two failed, and the failures are the better half of the result.

## Row 2 — the criterion passed a falsifiable test

The spherical cavity recodes to **m′ ≤ 2ℓ′ + 2** — single-argument, so the criterion predicted a genuine lattice where the rectangular one gave only a semilattice. It does:

| | Λ_cav (rect) | Λ_sph |
|---|---|---|
| pairs tested | 15,400 | **114,960** |
| join failures | 0 | **0** |
| meet failures | **768** | **0** |
| rank-modularity violations | n/a | **0** |
| distributivity violations | n/a | **0** / 216,000 triples |

480 cells, height 22, Sperner width 41, E(X) = 0. **The criterion predicted the outcome in advance from the arity of the cap alone, and got it right in both directions.** That is what makes it a criterion rather than an observation.

## And then the cap turned out to be Λ's cap

m′ ≤ 2ℓ′ + 2 gives 2ℓ+1 values of m. Λ's one coupling is k ≤ 4ℓ + 2 = **2(2ℓ+1)**.

The electromagnetic cavity carries the *same angular-momentum cap as the atom, without the factor of two.* And the missing two is not missing — it's the TE/TM axis, sitting beside the cap as a **free coordinate** instead of being multiplied into it.

That difference is visible in the constraint graph. Λ's is a connected tree (§3.5): the electron's spin multiplicity is folded into the cap, because Pauli couples it to ℓ. Λ_sph's is a **forest** — one edge ℓ′—m′, with t and n′ isolated — because the photon's polarization is coupled to nothing.

> **The connectivity of the constraint graph encodes exchange statistics.** Fermion: the multiplicity axis attaches, and the graph connects. Boson: it detaches, and the graph disconnects.

§6.5 already says the one coupling in Λ *is* the Pauli principle. This is the same statement read from the other side — the object where Pauli is absent has the coupling absent, in exactly the predicted place. Second route, no shared step (B.2.8).

## Row 1 — the ℓ-axis has its own domain, and it is B.2.2 again

ΔT along ℓ is **2RΔδ/ν³** — exact-ratio 0.9958 at n=5 rising to 0.9997 at n=80. So the admissibility test is:

**r_ℓ = 2RΔδ_ℓ / (ν³σ) ≥ 5**

which is B.2.2 with **Z² → Δδ**. Same functional form, same ν⁻³ exponent, different numerator. Committed as D2 before computing; confirmed.

The consequence is quantitative. At σ = 0.01 cm⁻¹ for Na:

| axis | Δδ | exits at ν |
|---|---|---|
| n | — | **163.7** |
| ℓ (s–p) | 0.500 | 130.0 |
| ℓ (p–d) | 0.835 | 154.2 |
| ℓ (d–f) | 0.014 | **39.5** |

Ratio n-axis to d–f is **4.149**, against the predicted (Z²/Δδ)^⅓ = **4.149**. Exact.

So the amendment writes itself, and it is small: **Rule 1 may admit ℓ-neighbours, subject to a Rule-4-form test with Z² replaced by Δδ_ℓ.** The ℓ-axis is a shorter axis, not a forbidden one, and *how much* shorter is computable per pair from the defects alone. §16.10.4's "the admissibility rule generalises" arriving a third time, now on a new axis.

Note the direction: the ℓ-bracket survives **longest** for the penetrating low-ℓ pairs, where the defects differ most, and dies first for the near-degenerate high-ℓ ones. That is the physically right answer, and it is the opposite of what I guessed.

## The tightening is generic, ~2×

| object | cells | narrower on | mean ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Λ_cav (rectangular) | 343 | 82.8% | 0.549 |
| Λ (Na, illustrative) | 15 | 15/15 | ~0.52 |
| Λ_sph TE | 12 | 12/12 | **0.407** |
| Λ_sph TM | 12 | 12/12 | **0.389** |

Four independent objects, all landing near a factor of two. The lattice bracket adds a second constraint of comparable strength on each side, and roughly halves the interval. Not object-specific — geometric.

## Withdrawals

**D4 — withdrawn.** I predicted the tightening concentrates where Δδ is smallest. It doesn't: ratios sit near 0.5 for Δδ = 0.835 *and* Δδ = 0.014, and the trends run in opposite directions with n. Δδ governs where the ℓ-axis **exits**, not where it **gains**. Those are different quantities and I conflated them. What it excludes: any account of the tightening that runs through defect size. Kind: structural.

**S3 — partial.** F(−1) = 0 was right, and my stated cause (free binary axis, 1 + (−1) = 0) is *sufficient* but not the operative one — removing the type axis still gives 0, by cap parity. So F(−1) = 0 here is overdetermined. This strengthens last session's negative: **F(−1) is parity-sensitive and a weak invariant.** Λ's stable F(−1) = 2 is more unusual than it looks.

## Where this leaves the grid

Two rows closed. The re-enumeration:

- **The ℓ-monotonicity condition** — now derived, with a bound. Remaining cell: the ablation on real channels, which needs your collection. That is the only thing standing between the lattice bracket and Rule 1.
- **The statistics/connectivity claim** is one comparison old. It wants a third object where the multiplicity axis is neither Pauli-coupled nor free — a **cylindrical** cavity, where m is capped by nothing but the geometry degenerates in pairs, or better, a **fermionic** photon-analogue if one exists in the book's Λ₉ target-spin extension. Λ₉ is the natural test: it added a *spin* axis. If the connectivity claim is right, Λ₉'s new axis should attach, not detach — and you have already confirmed the constraint graph stays a tree. **That is the claim already passing a test you ran for another reason**, which is worth checking properly rather than accepting.
- **The slack conjecture** is untouched and still the highest-value item, because it is the one that turns the New Law into an expression.

My recommendation: the Λ₉ connectivity check first — it is a re-read of results you already hold, no new computation — then the ablation when the collection is to hand.

## The slack conjecture resolves, and it turns on one thing

**A lemma, verified.** If an index factors as A × C_k with C_k a free chain of k values, then F(−1) = F_A(−1) · (0 if k even, 1 if odd). Checked over k = 2…6 and every cap 0…6, no exceptions.

The contrapositive is the usable form:

> **F(−1) ≠ 0 ⟹ the index has no detached factor of even extent.**

Apply it to Λ. **F(−1) = 2 ≠ 0, so Λ has no free axis of even extent** — no detached polarization-like factor, no undetermined binary freedom. That is not a new computation. It is the book's own number, and it has been sitting there as a structural theorem read only as a curiosity. §6.8.1 gives F(−1) = 2 a cause; this gives it a *use*.

## The kernel table, and the thing that surprised me

| object | the identity | kernel | dim | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ampère → Maxwell | ∇·∇× = 0 | all curls | **∞** | **incomplete** — covariance supplied externally |
| Λ_cav | ∇·E = 0 | transverse plane | 2 | complete; slack = polarization |
| Λ_sph | ∇·E = 0 + sphere BCs | TE / TM | 2 | complete; slack = the free C₂ axis |
| Λ | **none — order-realised** | — | 0 | complete; slack 0; graph connected |

The three EM rows carry **the same identity**. ∇·E = 0 and ∇·∇× = 0 are one condition. Maxwell's kernel is infinite because it is taken over the whole field space; the cavity's is 2 because the index **fixes k**, making the kernel pointwise.

> The difference between "Maxwell needed help from outside" and "the cavity index closed itself" is not a difference of identity. It is a difference of whether the index is discrete.

**Discretising the index is what makes identity-realised closure complete.** That is the mechanism the New Law has been missing, and it is why an *index* can do something a *field theory* cannot — which is a fair statement of what the whole book has been claiming, arrived at from a direction the book didn't take.

## The law, with an expression

The New Law had a clause — "realised in the object's own structure" — doing unexamined work. It now has two modes and a number:

- **Order-realised.** ℛ_int is the object's own order. slack = 0. Constraint graph connected. F(−1) unconstrained. *Λ.*
- **Identity-realised.** ℛ_int = ker of an internal identity D∘C = 0. Closure completes **iff dim ker D < ∞**, and the kernel then appears as a detached factor of exactly that extent. slack = dim ker D. *Maxwell, Λ_cav, Λ_sph.*

**slack(X) = dim ker ℛ_int**, with self-closure complete iff finite.

That is candidate-expression shape — what B.1 requires before anything joins the formalised list. It also absorbs the constraint-graph finding from last session rather than sitting beside it: the detached factor *is* the kernel, so "the graph disconnects for bosons" and "the slack is the polarization" are one statement.

## A correction to last session's withdrawal

I withdrew S3's *mechanism* — I'd claimed F(−1) = 0 in Λ_sph came from the free C₂ axis, then found it was 0 with the axis removed. Isolating properly: at even LMAX the coupled part gives F(−1) = 1, and multiplying by the free C₂ sends it to 0, every time.

**The mechanism was right. What was wrong was testing it at a cap where a second cause was also firing.** The withdrawal stands as written — I asserted a cause without isolating it, which is the error — but the cause itself survives. Two effects at one cap, and I read the sum as one.

## What this does not establish

Four objects. The identity-realised side has three; the order-realised side has **one**, which is Λ itself. So "order-realised ⟹ slack 0" rests on a single instance and could easily be a property of Λ rather than of orders. That is the weakest joint, and it is load-bearing for the law.

The Λ₉ check remains blocked, ρ = 1, reopening on re-upload. Its value is unchanged: if the target-spin axis attaches, the statistics/connectivity claim gets a second instance; if it runs free, the claim is refuted with one look.

## The next row, and it is cheap

The discriminating test is an index whose kernel is **odd**-dimensional. Scalar acoustic modes in the same spherical cavity: no polarization, kernel dim 1, no detached even factor — so the framework predicts **F(−1) ≠ 0 where the electromagnetic cavity gives 0**, on geometry that is otherwise identical.

Same box, same (ℓ, m, n), same cap m′ ≤ 2ℓ′+2. Only the field's vector character differs. If F(−1) doesn't move, the connection between kernel parity and F(−1) is coincidence and the lemma is doing no physical work. If it does move, the slack expression has a second independent confirmation and the acoustic case becomes the control that the EM cases lacked.

It costs one build, it needs no retrieval, and unlike the last three predictions I cannot call it from the armchair — the coupled part's F(−1) alternates with cap parity, so the answer depends on which cap the physics actually imposes.

## The slack conjecture resolves, and it turns on one thing

**A lemma, verified.** If an index factors as A × C_k with C_k a free chain of k values, then F(−1) = F_A(−1) · (0 if k even, 1 if odd). Checked over k = 2…6 and every cap 0…6, no exceptions.

The contrapositive is the usable form:

> **F(−1) ≠ 0 ⟹ the index has no detached factor of even extent.**

Apply it to Λ. **F(−1) = 2 ≠ 0, so Λ has no free axis of even extent** — no detached polarization-like factor, no undetermined binary freedom. That is not a new computation. It is the book's own number, and it has been sitting there as a structural theorem read only as a curiosity. §6.8.1 gives F(−1) = 2 a cause; this gives it a *use*.

## The kernel table, and the thing that surprised me

| object | the identity | kernel | dim | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ampère → Maxwell | ∇·∇× = 0 | all curls | **∞** | **incomplete** — covariance supplied externally |
| Λ_cav | ∇·E = 0 | transverse plane | 2 | complete; slack = polarization |
| Λ_sph | ∇·E = 0 + sphere BCs | TE / TM | 2 | complete; slack = the free C₂ axis |
| Λ | **none — order-realised** | — | 0 | complete; slack 0; graph connected |

The three EM rows carry **the same identity**. ∇·E = 0 and ∇·∇× = 0 are one condition. Maxwell's kernel is infinite because it is taken over the whole field space; the cavity's is 2 because the index **fixes k**, making the kernel pointwise.

> The difference between "Maxwell needed help from outside" and "the cavity index closed itself" is not a difference of identity. It is a difference of whether the index is discrete.

**Discretising the index is what makes identity-realised closure complete.** That is the mechanism the New Law has been missing, and it is why an *index* can do something a *field theory* cannot — which is a fair statement of what the whole book has been claiming, arrived at from a direction the book didn't take.

## The law, with an expression

The New Law had a clause — "realised in the object's own structure" — doing unexamined work. It now has two modes and a number:

- **Order-realised.** ℛ_int is the object's own order. slack = 0. Constraint graph connected. F(−1) unconstrained. *Λ.*
- **Identity-realised.** ℛ_int = ker of an internal identity D∘C = 0. Closure completes **iff dim ker D < ∞**, and the kernel then appears as a detached factor of exactly that extent. slack = dim ker D. *Maxwell, Λ_cav, Λ_sph.*

**slack(X) = dim ker ℛ_int**, with self-closure complete iff finite.

That is candidate-expression shape — what B.1 requires before anything joins the formalised list. It also absorbs the constraint-graph finding from last session rather than sitting beside it: the detached factor *is* the kernel, so "the graph disconnects for bosons" and "the slack is the polarization" are one statement.

## A correction to last session's withdrawal

I withdrew S3's *mechanism* — I'd claimed F(−1) = 0 in Λ_sph came from the free C₂ axis, then found it was 0 with the axis removed. Isolating properly: at even LMAX the coupled part gives F(−1) = 1, and multiplying by the free C₂ sends it to 0, every time.

**The mechanism was right. What was wrong was testing it at a cap where a second cause was also firing.** The withdrawal stands as written — I asserted a cause without isolating it, which is the error — but the cause itself survives. Two effects at one cap, and I read the sum as one.

## What this does not establish

Four objects. The identity-realised side has three; the order-realised side has **one**, which is Λ itself. So "order-realised ⟹ slack 0" rests on a single instance and could easily be a property of Λ rather than of orders. That is the weakest joint, and it is load-bearing for the law.

The Λ₉ check remains blocked, ρ = 1, reopening on re-upload. Its value is unchanged: if the target-spin axis attaches, the statistics/connectivity claim gets a second instance; if it runs free, the claim is refuted with one look.

## The next row, and it is cheap

The discriminating test is an index whose kernel is **odd**-dimensional. Scalar acoustic modes in the same spherical cavity: no polarization, kernel dim 1, no detached even factor — so the framework predicts **F(−1) ≠ 0 where the electromagnetic cavity gives 0**, on geometry that is otherwise identical.

Same box, same (ℓ, m, n), same cap m′ ≤ 2ℓ′+2. Only the field's vector character differs. If F(−1) doesn't move, the connection between kernel parity and F(−1) is coincidence and the lemma is doing no physical work. If it does move, the slack expression has a second independent confirmation and the acoustic case becomes the control that the EM cases lacked.

It costs one build, it needs no retrieval, and unlike the last three predictions I cannot call it from the armchair — the coupled part's F(−1) alternates with cap parity, so the answer depends on which cap the physics actually imposes.
